quests.instruction: After dinner, Mum asks Sara to ___ the dishes.
quests.hint: Think about a chore, not about creating something.
quests.explanation: Do goes with chores and tasks such as the dishes, the shopping or homework. Make is for creating something, like a cake.
quests.funFact: We do homework, but we make a mistake.

quests.instruction: Aisha has just ___ a beautiful card for her grandmother out of coloured paper.
quests.hint: She created something new.
quests.explanation: Make means to create or produce something. 'Do' is more often used for activities and tasks.
quests.funFact: 'Make' is used with food, plans and noise; 'do' is used with work and chores.

quests.instruction: Dad says, 'First, you must ___ your homework, and then you can play.'
quests.hint: It is a task that has to be completed.
quests.explanation: Do is used for tasks, jobs and activities, like homework, the dishes or the shopping.
quests.funFact: People say 'do the dishes', but they say 'make a cake'.

quests.instruction: The teacher claps twice, and the noisy room becomes quiet. Now the lesson can ___.
quests.hint: Everyone is ready for something to get going.
quests.explanation: Begin and start both mean to get something going. Begin is common for lessons, stories and big events.
quests.funFact: 'Begin' can sound a little more formal than 'start'.

quests.instruction: Dad turns the key and tries to ___ the car, but the engine does not wake up.
quests.hint: It is about a machine that must come alive.
quests.explanation: Start can be used for machines or engines. You start a car, but you do not usually 'begin' a car.
quests.funFact: Many modern cars start with a button instead of a key.

quests.instruction: The story ___ with the words, 'Once upon a time, in a village by the sea.'
quests.hint: It is about the very first words.
quests.explanation: Begin means to be the first part of something. A story begins at the first words and ends at the last.
quests.funFact: Many stories in English-speaking countries begin with 'Once upon a time'.

quests.instruction: When Kofi has ___ his drawing, he will show it to the whole class.
quests.hint: The drawing is complete.
quests.explanation: Finish means to complete something so that nothing more needs to be done.
quests.funFact: In English, 'finish' is often followed by '-ing': finish reading, finish eating.

quests.instruction: The school year will ___ in June, and then the summer holidays begin.
quests.hint: It describes a period of time that comes to a close.
quests.explanation: End means to come to a close. A film or a school year ends, and a person finishes a task.
quests.funFact: 'The end' appears at the close of many stories and films.

quests.instruction: It seemed as if the rain would never ___, so the match was cancelled.
quests.hint: The rain keeps falling, and it does not come to a halt.
quests.explanation: Stop means to not continue. Rain stops, but people finish tasks.
quests.funFact: 'Stop' is one of the first words that many people learn in a new language because of road signs.

quests.instruction: The menu has three desserts, and Hana is taking a long time to ___ one.
quests.hint: She looks at all of them before taking one.
quests.explanation: Choose means to pick one thing from several. Decide is about making up your mind.
quests.funFact: Many children's menus offer a choice of two or three things.

quests.instruction: Mum cannot ___ whether to paint the kitchen green or yellow. She keeps changing her mind.
quests.hint: The problem is that she cannot make up her mind.
quests.explanation: Decide means to settle on an answer after thinking. You decide whether to do something; you choose between things.
quests.funFact: 'Decide' is followed by 'to' or 'whether'.

quests.instruction: The teacher says, 'Please ___ a partner and sit together.'
quests.hint: The class must pick one person from among others.
quests.explanation: Choose takes an object: choose a partner, a book or a team.
quests.funFact: The word 'choose' has a long 'oo' sound, like 'moon'.

quests.instruction: A group of children use bricks, wood and nails to ___ a small hut in the garden.
quests.hint: They put materials together to make a structure.
quests.explanation: Build means to make something big or solid by putting parts together, like a house or a hut.
quests.funFact: Birds build nests using twigs, mud and leaves.

quests.instruction: Using only words and her imagination, Mia can ___ an entirely new story about a flying whale.
quests.hint: It makes something that did not exist before.
quests.explanation: Create means to make something new from your own ideas. Authors and artists create.
quests.funFact: Create can be used for art, music, stories and even new games.

quests.instruction: Practising every day will help Zoe ___ her confidence, one step at a time.
quests.hint: Think about something that grows stronger bit by bit.
quests.explanation: Build can also describe something that grows stronger slowly, like confidence, a habit or a friendship.
quests.funFact: Friendships are often said to be built on trust.

quests.instruction: Anu ran as fast as she could but still ___ the bus, and she had to wait for the next one.
quests.hint: She was too late to catch it.
quests.explanation: Miss means to fail to catch or meet something. You miss a bus. You lose something that you owned.
quests.funFact: 'Miss' can also mean that you feel sad when someone is away.

quests.instruction: Max put his gloves down somewhere in the park, and now he cannot find them. He ___ his gloves.
quests.hint: They are gone, and he does not know where.
quests.explanation: Lose means to no longer have something because you cannot find it. 'Lose' also means to not win.
quests.funFact: 'Lose' has one 'o', and 'loose' has two and sounds different.

quests.instruction: Two football teams are playing. The team with the most goals will ___ the match.
quests.hint: It is about who comes first.
quests.explanation: Win is used with the prize or game: win a game, win a medal. 'Beat' is used with the opponent: beat the other team.
quests.funFact: You win a game, but you beat a person or a team.

quests.instruction: Our team played really well and ___ the other team by three goals.
quests.hint: The opponent is the object of the verb.
quests.explanation: Beat means to do better than another person or team. After 'beat', you name the loser.
quests.funFact: A beating heart is the same word, but its meaning is different.

quests.instruction: Every morning the sun ___ in the east, and every evening it sets.
quests.hint: It moves up on its own.
quests.explanation: Rise means to go up by itself. Raise means to lift something up. The sun rises, but you raise your hand.
quests.funFact: 'Rise' never has an object: the sun rises, but you raise your hand.

quests.instruction: To ask a question, Leo ___ his hand and waits for the teacher.
quests.hint: He is the one lifting.
quests.explanation: Raise means to lift something up. It needs an object: raise your hand.
quests.funFact: Raise can also mean to bring up a child or collect money: raise funds.

quests.instruction: Tom's mother wants a new bike, so every month she will ___ a little money in a jar.
quests.hint: She puts some money aside for later.
quests.explanation: Save means to put money aside for later. Keep means to hold on to something and not give it away.
quests.funFact: If you save a seat, you keep it free for someone.

quests.instruction: Dad asks, 'Can you ___ me a seat next to you on the bus?' He does not want anyone else to sit there.
quests.hint: Someone will arrive later.
quests.explanation: Save a seat means to keep it free for someone who is coming later.
quests.funFact: 'Save' also means to rescue: a lifeguard can save a swimmer.

quests.instruction: The lifeguard jumps into the water and quickly pulls out a child who was in danger. He ___ the child.
quests.hint: He rescued someone from danger.
quests.explanation: Save has several meanings: to rescue, to put aside money and to keep a seat. This one means rescuing someone.
quests.funFact: Lifeguards are trained to save people, as well as to prevent accidents.

quests.instruction: Rani puts her fingers on the side of a warm cup and feels the heat. She uses her sense of ___.
quests.hint: It comes through her skin.
quests.explanation: Touch is a sense of the skin. You touch a surface and you feel what it is like.
quests.funFact: Your fingertips are among the most sensitive parts of your body.

quests.instruction: Before serving the soup, Zoe puts a tiny spoonful in her mouth to find out if it needs more salt. She wants to ___ it.
quests.hint: She is trying out the flavour on her tongue.
quests.explanation: Taste is the sense you use with your tongue. You taste food to learn its flavour.
quests.funFact: Many flavours that we notice come from smell rather than taste.

quests.instruction: The fresh bread by the window is so lovely that Dev can ___ it from the garden.
quests.hint: It reaches him through the air.
quests.explanation: Smell is the sense of the nose. You can smell something without touching it.
quests.funFact: A dog's sense of smell is many times better than a human's.

quests.instruction: Nina's grandmother ___ the old photograph to see how soft the paper was.
quests.hint: She used her fingers.
quests.explanation: Touch means to put a hand or finger on something. It does not mean looking.
quests.funFact: 'Touch' can also mean to make someone feel strong emotion: the film touched us.

quests.instruction: Ella has a cold, and her nose is blocked, so she cannot ___ the flowers.
quests.hint: Her nose does the work.
quests.explanation: Smell means to notice something using your nose. A blocked nose is the cause here.
quests.funFact: Colds can take away your sense of smell for a short time.

quests.instruction: With his eyes closed, Raj puts his hand on the cat's back and can ___ it purring.
quests.hint: His eyes are closed, so another sense helps him.
quests.explanation: Feel means to notice through touch, such as the purr of a cat under your hand.
quests.funFact: A cat's purr can sometimes be felt as a gentle vibration.
